reading.title: Maya und Lena
reading.intro: Maya has been in Berlin for three days. She is at a café table on the Bergmannstraße, and the woman at the next table says hello.
reading.photos[0].caption: Der U-Bahnhof Französische Straße: Maya wohnt in Mitte.
reading.photos[1].caption: Ein Döner am Kottbusser Tor. Lena isst hier oft.
reading.en: Lena: Hi! Is the chair free? · Maya: Yes, please. Hi! · Lena: My name is Lena. And you? · Maya: I'm Maya. I come from Canada. · Lena: From Canada! And you live in Berlin? · Maya: Yes, in Mitte. Three days. My German is … small. · Lena: Your German is good! I come from Austria, from Vienna. I'm a student. · Maya: What do you study? · Lena: Music. And you? Are you a student? · Maya: No, I'm a teacher. English. · Waiter: Good evening. What would you like? · Maya: A coffee, please. – Lena, why does he say “Sie”? · Lena: He is the waiter. You are the customer. That's polite. We say “du”.
reading.fact: Berliners say *Hallo* to the bus driver and *Tschüss* to the cashier. Not saying it is the one thing that counts as rude.
reading.tasks[1].instruction: Maya, Lena or the waiter? Write the name.

grammar[0].blocks[0].title: Introduce yourself
grammar[0].blocks[0].note: Ask a friend with *du*, a stranger with *Sie*. The answer is the same.
grammar[0].blocks[1].blocks[0].title: Who is who
grammar[0].blocks[2].blocks[0].title: du or Sie?
grammar[0].blocks[2].blocks[0].note: Not sure? Say *Sie* — and wait for “Wir können du sagen”.
grammar[0].blocks[2].blocks[0].root.q: A friend, family, a child or another learner?
grammar[0].blocks[2].blocks[1].title: sie, sie or Sie?
grammar[0].blocks[2].blocks[1].text: *sie* is she, *sie* is they, and *Sie* with a capital S is the polite you. The verb gives it away: sie *ist* (she is), sie *sind* (they are), Sie *sind* (you are).
grammar[0].fact: *du* or *Sie*? When in doubt, *Sie*. The other person will say *Wir können uns duzen*, and from then on it is *du* for life.

grammar[1].blocks[3].title: Hallo at every hour
grammar[1].fact: *Moin* is hello in Hamburg at any hour, *Servus* in Munich, *Grüß Gott* in Austria. *Hallo* works everywhere, and *Guten Tag* when you want to be safe.

document.caption: Ein Klingelschild in Berlin: Wer wohnt hier?
document.intro: The name plate at the front door of a Berlin house. Every flat has a bell and a name; two names means two people share. Read the names and answer.
document.fact: Germans write their surname on the bell, the letterbox and often the door, so the postman finds them. Many flats have no number at all: the name is the address.
document.tasks[0].instruction: Find the answer on the name plate.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Circle the question that fits the answer.
document.tasks[2].instruction: Write your own name as it would stand on the bell, and the name of one neighbour.
